title: t00 What Is AI
tagline: Most of today's AI isn't built on rules people write. It learns patterns from examples.

items.title: Your phone can find
items.subtitle: Your phone can find your cat in your photos, yet nobody ever gave it rules for what a cat looks like.

items.title: So how does it do it?
items.subtitle: So how does it do it? It saw tons of examples and worked out the patterns itself. That's today's AI.

items.title: A traditional program works differently:
items.subtitle: A traditional program works differently: people write the rules one by one, and the computer follows them.

items.title: For payroll or booking flights
items.subtitle: For payroll or booking flights, the rules are clear, so that's enough.

items.title: But some things are hard
items.subtitle: But some things are hard to write rules for, like reading a handwritten three. Fat, skinny, tilted, you know it instantly.

items.title: Now try writing down how.
items.subtitle: Now try writing down how. "Two curves stacked"? So is an eight. "Bottom half opens left"? So does a five.

items.title: Rules like that miss some threes
items.subtitle: Rules like that miss some threes and mistake other digits for threes.

items.title: So most of today's AI flips it around:
items.subtitle: So most of today's AI flips it around: no rules, just examples.

items.title: Show the computer hundreds
items.subtitle: Show the computer hundreds or thousands of handwritten digits, each with its answer: this is a three, this is a seven.

items.title: It finds the patterns itself
items.subtitle: It finds the patterns itself, and that's called machine learning.

items.title: What it learns is called a model.
items.subtitle: What it learns is called a model. Show the model a new image, and it gives you an answer.

items.title: A lot of people think programmers
items.subtitle: A lot of people think programmers coded in everything AI can do. Mostly, it learned from examples, which we call data.

items.title: Let's actually try it
items.subtitle: Let's actually try it, with nearly 1,800 handwritten digits, each a tiny 8×8 grid.

items.title: First we lock away 300 as the test
items.subtitle: First we lock away 300 as the test, and the rest are examples to learn from.

items.title: Learning from them is called training
items.subtitle: Learning from them is called training, and during training it never sees a test question.

items.title: Only questions it hasn't seen can
items.subtitle: Only questions it hasn't seen can show whether it truly learned, or just memorized.

items.title: So, take a guess:
items.subtitle: So, take a guess: with just 10 examples, how much of the test does it get right?

items.title: Pick ten at random
items.subtitle: Pick ten at random, and often some digits don't show up at all.

items.title: We tried twenty different
items.subtitle: We tried twenty different random sets of ten. The typical score was about 37%: better than the 10% you'd get guessing, but still low.

items.title: With a hundred examples, it gets 88%.
items.subtitle: With a hundred examples, it gets 88%. With all 1,500 or so, it gets 97%.

items.title: We never gave it rules for a three
items.subtitle: We never gave it rules for a three, just told it which ones were threes. In this experiment, more examples meant better scores.

items.title: Still, it missed 10 of the 300
items.subtitle: Still, it missed 10 of the 300, like this messy two it called a one.

items.title: Here's another way to see it:
items.subtitle: Here's another way to see it: today's AI is a prediction machine. Not predicting the future, just seeing something and guessing the answer.

items.title: Our model also says how sure it is.
items.subtitle: Our model also says how sure it is. It's 96% sure this one's a three.

items.title: Other AI works the same way.
items.subtitle: Other AI works the same way. Give a language model half a sentence, and it guesses the next word, then the next, until there's a whole answer.

items.title: Chatbots built on large
items.subtitle: Chatbots built on large language models reply this way.

items.title: They guess well
items.subtitle: They guess well, but a convincing answer can still be wrong.

items.title: So how do all these terms fit together?
items.subtitle: So how do all these terms fit together? Picture AI, artificial intelligence, as the biggest circle: computers doing things that seem to take smarts.

items.title: A chess program built
items.subtitle: A chess program built on hand-written rules counts as AI. A plain payroll program doesn't.

items.title: Inside AI is machine learning
items.subtitle: Inside AI is machine learning, and inside that, deep learning, which runs on neural networks: many layers of simple math.

items.title: "Deep" just means many layers
items.subtitle: "Deep" just means many layers, not deep understanding. Large language models are built with deep learning.

items.title: When I say "today's AI,"
items.subtitle: When I say "today's AI," I mean machine learning: AI that learns from examples.

items.title: Learning from data can go wrong, too.
items.subtitle: Learning from data can go wrong, too. According to Reuters, Amazon once tried using AI to screen résumés.

items.title: It learned from 10 years
items.subtitle: It learned from 10 years of résumés sent to the company, mostly by men.

items.title: In effect, it taught itself that male
items.subtitle: In effect, it taught itself that male candidates were better.

items.title: Résumés with the word "women's,"
items.subtitle: Résumés with the word "women's," as in "women's chess club captain," got marked down.

items.title: The tool was later scrapped.
items.subtitle: The tool was later scrapped. If the data is biased, the model can pick that up too.

items.title: When you use AI, remember three things.
items.subtitle: When you use AI, remember three things.

items.title: First, it may answer anyway
items.subtitle: First, it may answer anyway, even about things it's never seen. Show our digit model the letter A, and it still has to pick from zero to nine.

items.title: It says it's 92% sure that's a four.
items.subtitle: It says it's 92% sure that's a four. But it can only pick from the ten digits.

items.title: A kid would say
items.subtitle: A kid would say, "That's not a number." The model won't.

items.title: Second, it gives you predictions
items.subtitle: Second, it gives you predictions, not the truth. Remember that messy two? The model was 81% sure it was a one, and it was wrong.

items.title: Third, what it gets right or wrong
items.subtitle: Third, what it gets right or wrong depends on its data, and also on how it's designed and trained.

items.title: So to judge whether an AI is reliable
items.subtitle: So to judge whether an AI is reliable, first find out what data it learned from.

items.title: Whenever an AI sounds totally sure, ask yourself:
items.subtitle: Whenever an AI sounds totally sure, ask yourself: has it seen questions like this before?

items.title: Most of today's AI isn't
items.subtitle: Most of today's AI isn't built on rules people write. It learns patterns from examples.

items.subtitle: Next time, we'll look at why a model can ace the practice questions and still stumble on new ones. That's often a sign of overfitting.
